titleEn: Give ear, my people, to my teaching
progression: | Dm Dm | Gm Dm | Dm A7 | Dm Dm |
intro: Seventy-two verses, the second longest psalm in the book, and the only one that tells the whole national story from the exodus to the choice of David. It opens like a teacher, not like a singer: listen, incline your ear, I will speak in a parable. Then it runs the wilderness generation through a cycle that repeats four or five times, rescue, forgetting, craving, anger, mercy, and it does not resolve the cycle so much as relocate it, ending at Zion and at a shepherd from the sheepfolds. For a learner it is the best place in the psalter to watch the vav-consecutive narrative past at work: verse after verse begins with the same prefix and the same jolt forward in time.

stichs.en: A maskil of Asaph.
Give ear, my people, to my teaching;
incline your ear to the words of my mouth.

verses.summary: The psalm opens as instruction, not as prayer. Nothing is addressed to God in these first four verses; the audience is the people, and the speaker claims the authority of a teacher.

stichs.en: I will open my mouth with a parable;
I will pour out riddles from long ago.

verses.summary: History is announced as a riddle. What follows is a plain narrative, so the difficulty is not in the events but in what they mean, which is the problem the psalm sets its listener.

stichs.en: What we have heard and come to know,
and our fathers told us.

verses.summary: The chain of transmission is named before any content is transmitted. Knowledge here arrives by ear, from the previous link, not by witness.

stichs.en: We will not hide it from their children, from the coming generation,
telling the praises of the LORD, and His strength, and the wonders He did.

verses.summary: The obligation runs forward, not backward. Having received, the generation now owes the telling, and hiding is named as the failure mode.

stichs.en: He set up a testimony in Jacob,
and placed a teaching in Israel,
which He commanded our fathers to make known to their children,

verses.summary: The teaching is not the teacher's private idea. It was commanded, and the command included its own transmission, which makes forgetting a breach rather than an accident.

stichs.en: so that the coming generation would know, children yet to be born,
who would rise and tell their own children,

verses.summary: Three generations are stacked in one verse: the fathers, the children, and children not yet born. The purpose clause reaches past everyone alive.

stichs.en: so they would put their confidence in God,
and not forget the deeds of God,
and would keep His commandments.

verses.summary: The aim of the telling is stated in three verbs: trust, do not forget, keep. Memory sits in the middle, holding the other two together.

stichs.en: and would not be like their fathers,
a stubborn and rebellious generation,
a generation that did not set its heart right,
whose spirit was not faithful to God.

verses.summary: The frame ends by naming the counter-example, and it is the fathers themselves. The same ancestors who transmitted the teaching in verse 3 are the warning in verse 8.

stichs.en: The sons of Ephraim, armed, shooting the bow,
turned back on the day of battle.

verses.summary: An abrupt cut from instruction to a single tribe and a defeat the psalm never explains. It functions as a headline for everything the narrative is about to unfold.

stichs.en: They did not keep the covenant of God,
and refused to walk in His teaching.

verses.summary: The military failure is immediately reread as a covenantal one. The psalm gives no tactical account of the rout because it is not interested in one.

stichs.en: They forgot His deeds,
and the wonders He had shown them.

verses.summary: Forgetting is the hinge word of the whole psalm, and it lands here for the first time as an accomplished fact rather than a risk.

stichs.en: In front of their fathers He did a wonder,
in the land of Egypt, the field of Zoan.

verses.summary: The narrative proper begins, and it begins by insisting on eyewitness: this happened in front of them. What was forgotten was not hearsay.

stichs.en: He split the sea and brought them across,
and made the waters stand like a heap.

verses.summary: Two verbs of splitting will govern this psalm, one for the sea and one for the rock. Both make a way through something solid.

stichs.en: He led them with a cloud by day,
and all the night with a light of fire.

verses.summary: Day and night are covered by the same guidance, in two forms. The verse is built as a pair, and the pairing is the point.

stichs.en: He split rocks in the wilderness,
and gave them drink as from the great deeps.

verses.summary: The word for the primeval deep is used for drinking water in a desert, which is a deliberate excess: not enough, but more than could be asked.

stichs.en: He brought streams out of a rock,
and brought waters down like rivers.

verses.summary: The water miracle is told twice, in verse 15 and again here, before the complaint arrives. The abundance is established so the next verse can be measured against it.

stichs.en: But they went on sinning against Him,
rebelling against the Most High in the parched land.

verses.summary: The turn is marked by a verb that means to add, to do more of the same. The rebellion is presented as accumulation, not as a single lapse.

stichs.en: They tested God in their heart,
asking food for their appetite.

verses.summary: The offence is not hunger but testing. The request is real and the psalm still calls it a trial set for God, because of what the heart was doing while the mouth asked.

stichs.en: They spoke against God; they said,
Can God set a table in the wilderness?

verses.summary: The complaint is quoted rather than described, so the reader hears the sarcasm directly. A table in a wilderness is exactly the image the psalm will grant them.

stichs.en: Look, He struck a rock and water gushed, and streams overflowed.
Can He give bread as well?
Or provide meat for His people?

verses.summary: The people argue from the miracle they have just received to the miracle they doubt. Their evidence is sound and their conclusion is the opposite of trust.

stichs.en: Therefore the LORD heard and was enraged,
and a fire was kindled against Jacob,
and anger also rose against Israel.

verses.summary: The response is to the speech, not to the appetite. God heard, which puts the offence in verse 19 and not in verse 18.

stichs.en: because they did not believe in God,
and did not trust in His salvation.

verses.summary: The verse supplies the charge in plain terms, twice over. Two verbs of trust are negated, and nothing else is alleged.

stichs.en: Yet He commanded the skies above,
and opened the doors of heaven.

verses.summary: Immediately after the anger, the giving resumes. The psalm does not soften the sequence or explain it away; the two simply follow each other.

stichs.en: He rained manna on them to eat,
and gave them the grain of heaven.

verses.summary: Food falls like weather. The verb is the ordinary one for rain, which puts the manna in the same category as the hail that will fall on Egypt later in the psalm.

stichs.en: Each man ate the bread of the mighty;
He sent them provisions to the full.

verses.summary: The phrase rendered bread of the mighty is unusual and has been read in more than one way. Whatever it names, the point is that ordinary people ate it.

stichs.en: He set the east wind moving in the heavens,
and drove the south wind by His strength.

verses.summary: The meat arrives by meteorology rather than by miracle language. Two named winds do the work, and the verb for driving is the one used for herding animals.

stichs.en: He rained meat on them like dust,
and winged birds like the sand of the seas.

verses.summary: The two similes are the standard biblical images for uncountable multitude, and they are applied to a request that was meant to be impossible.

stichs.en: He made it fall inside their camp,
all around their dwellings.

verses.summary: Delivery is described with a precision the request never asked for: in the middle of the camp, and around every tent.

stichs.en: They ate and were well filled,
and He brought them what they craved.

verses.summary: The request is granted completely, in the exact words in which it was made. Getting what was craved is the setup for the next verse, not the resolution.

stichs.en: They had not yet turned from their craving,
their food still in their mouths,

verses.summary: The timing is the whole verse. Judgement arrives while the mouth is full, which collapses the distance between the gift and its consequence.

stichs.en: when the anger of God rose against them,
and killed among their strongest,
and brought down the young men of Israel.

verses.summary: The dead are the fittest and the youngest, which is the opposite of what a plague of appetite would be expected to take. The reversal is deliberate.

stichs.en: For all this they went on sinning,
and did not believe in His wonders.

verses.summary: The same verb of continuation from verse 17 returns, and it will return again. The psalm is showing a loop rather than a line.

stichs.en: So He ended their days in a breath,
and their years in sudden terror.

verses.summary: The word for breath is the one that dominates Ecclesiastes: vapour, nothing you can hold. A whole generation is spent as if it were that.

stichs.en: When He killed them, they would seek Him,
and turn back and search hard for God.

verses.summary: The verbs are iterative: this is what they did each time, not once. Repentance is presented as a reflex triggered by death, which is why the next verses distrust it.

stichs.en: They remembered that God was their rock,
and God Most High their redeemer.

verses.summary: Remembering appears here as the counterweight to the forgetting of verse 11, and the psalm will withdraw it in the very next line.

stichs.en: But they flattered Him with their mouth,
and lied to Him with their tongue.

verses.summary: The repentance of the previous two verses is retracted as verbal only. Mouth and tongue are named as the organs of the failure, echoing the mouth full of meat in verse 30.

stichs.en: Their heart was not steady with Him,
and they were not faithful to His covenant.

verses.summary: The wording deliberately repeats verse 8, heart and faithfulness both negated. The generation that was warned about the fathers has become them.

stichs.en: But He, being compassionate, would pardon guilt and not destroy;
again and again He turned His anger back,
and did not rouse all His wrath.

verses.summary: The pivot of the first half. The cycle does not break because the people change; it continues because the anger is repeatedly withdrawn short of its full extent.

stichs.en: He remembered that they were flesh,
a wind that goes and does not come back.

verses.summary: Now it is God who remembers, in the same verb the people used in verse 35. What He remembers is not their merit but their fragility.

stichs.en: How often they rebelled against Him in the wilderness,
and grieved Him in the wasteland.

verses.summary: An exclamation rather than a report, and the only place the psalm counts. The verb for grieving assigns pain to God, not just anger.

stichs.en: Again they tested God,
and set bounds for the Holy One of Israel.

verses.summary: The final verb of this verse is rare and its sense is argued over. On any reading the charge is that they drew a line around what God was allowed to be able to do.

stichs.en: They did not remember His hand,
the day He ransomed them from the adversary,

verses.summary: The failure to remember is what launches the second retelling. The psalm now goes back to Egypt and tells the plagues, which it had skipped the first time.

stichs.en: when He set His signs in Egypt,
and His portents in the field of Zoan.

verses.summary: The line repeats verse 12 almost word for word, which marks the start of the second cycle and tells the listener to compare the two.

stichs.en: He turned their canals to blood,
so they could not drink their streams.

verses.summary: The plague sequence opens with water made undrinkable, the exact inverse of the rock that gave drink in verses 15 and 16.

stichs.en: He sent swarms among them, and they devoured them,
and frogs, and they ruined them.

verses.summary: Two plagues in one verse, each with its own consuming verb. The psalm's list is shorter than the one in Exodus and in a different order.

stichs.en: He gave their produce to the grub,
and their labour to the locust.

verses.summary: Two different insect names in one line. Hebrew has several words for locust at different stages, and the parallelism is exploiting that vocabulary.

stichs.en: He killed their vines with hail,
and their sycamores with sleet.

verses.summary: The second noun here occurs nowhere else in the Bible, so its translation is a guess constrained only by the parallel with hail.

stichs.en: He handed their cattle over to the hail,
and their livestock to the lightning bolts.

verses.summary: The verb for handing over is a legal one, delivering a prisoner into custody. It will return in verse 62 with Israel as the prisoner.

stichs.en: He sent against them His burning anger,
fury and rage and trouble,
a deputation of messengers of evil.

verses.summary: Four nouns for anger stacked in one line, then a phrase that turns the emotions into a delegation with an errand.

stichs.en: He cleared a path for His anger;
He did not spare their soul from death,
and handed their life over to the plague.

verses.summary: The image is road building. Anger is given a level highway, the same word used elsewhere for preparing a way for a king.

stichs.en: He struck down every firstborn in Egypt,
the first of their strength in the tents of Ham.

verses.summary: The plague sequence ends where Exodus ends it. Egypt is called by the ancestral name Ham, which places the whole event in a genealogy.

stichs.en: He led His people out like sheep,
and drove them like a flock in the wilderness.

verses.summary: The shepherd image enters, and it will be the psalm's last image seventy-two verses in. Everything between here and David is held inside it.

stichs.en: He led them in safety and they were not afraid,
and the sea covered their enemies.

verses.summary: Two fates in one verse, arranged as a chiasm around the sea. The same water that made a road covers the pursuers.

stichs.en: He brought them to His holy border,
this mountain His right hand had won.

verses.summary: The demonstrative points at something the audience can see. The psalm is being said somewhere the mountain is in view, which locates the whole recital.

stichs.en: He drove out nations before them,
apportioned them an inheritance by the line,
and settled the tribes of Israel in their tents.

verses.summary: Conquest is described as surveying. A measuring line, not a sword, does the decisive work in this account of the land.

stichs.en: Yet they tested and defied God Most High,
and did not keep His testimonies.

verses.summary: The cycle restarts on the other side of the Jordan, with the same two verbs used of the wilderness. Arrival changed the setting and nothing else.

stichs.en: They fell back and betrayed like their fathers;
they twisted like a slack bow.

verses.summary: The bow returns from verse 9, now as a simile for the whole people. A bow that warps sends the arrow somewhere other than where it was aimed.

stichs.en: They angered Him with their high places,
and made Him jealous with their carved images.

verses.summary: The offence in the land is idolatry, not appetite. The psalm has moved from a hunger story to a worship story without changing its diagnosis.

stichs.en: God heard and was enraged,
and utterly rejected Israel.

verses.summary: The wording of verse 21 comes back, heard and enraged. What follows this time is not fire in the camp but the loss of the sanctuary.

stichs.en: He abandoned the dwelling at Shiloh,
the tent He had pitched among men.

verses.summary: A specific place with a known end. Shiloh housed the ark before Jerusalem, and its fall is the historical event this psalm is arguing from.

stichs.en: He gave His strength into captivity,
and His splendour into the hand of the adversary.

verses.summary: Strength and splendour stand in for the ark without naming it. The psalm says God handed it over, rather than that it was taken.

stichs.en: He handed His people over to the sword,
and was enraged with His own inheritance.

verses.summary: The legal verb from verse 48 returns, and this time the property delivered up is Israel. The word inheritance makes the loss self-inflicted.

stichs.en: Fire devoured his young men,
and his young women had no wedding song.

verses.summary: Catastrophe is measured by an absent ceremony. The verb in the second half is the one used for the songs sung to a bride.

stichs.en: His priests fell by the sword,
and his widows did not weep.

verses.summary: The silence is the horror. Either there was no one left to mourn or no time to, and the psalm does not choose between the two.

stichs.en: Then the Lord woke like a sleeper,
like a warrior shaking off wine.

verses.summary: The boldest image in the psalm, and it is offered without apology. Two similes, both of them about a delay that ends suddenly.

stichs.en: He beat His foes back,
and put a lasting disgrace on them.

verses.summary: The enemies are driven backward, the same direction Ephraim went in verse 9. The reversal is exact and probably intentional.

stichs.en: He rejected the tent of Joseph,
and did not choose the tribe of Ephraim.

verses.summary: The rescue does not restore the north. Shiloh was in Ephraim's territory, and the psalm says plainly that it was not rebuilt.

stichs.en: He chose the tribe of Judah,
Mount Zion, which He loved.

verses.summary: The choosing verb, negated in the previous verse, is now affirmative. Two lines decide between north and south, and the psalm gives no argument for the decision beyond love.

stichs.en: He built His sanctuary like the heights,
like the earth He founded forever.

verses.summary: The new sanctuary is compared to created things rather than to Shiloh. Permanence is claimed by analogy with the ground itself.

stichs.en: He chose David His servant,
and took him from the sheep pens.

verses.summary: David appears for the first and only time, seventy verses in, and he arrives as a job description rather than a biography.

stichs.en: From behind the nursing ewes He brought him,
to shepherd Jacob His people, Israel His inheritance.

verses.summary: The same verb of shepherding that described God in verse 52 is now handed to a man. The transfer is the psalm's answer to the whole preceding disaster.

stichs.en: He shepherded them with an upright heart,
and led them with skilful hands.

verses.summary: The last word of the psalm is the verb for leading used of God in verse 14 and verse 53. The problem named in verse 8 was a heart not set right, and the closing line answers it with a heart that is.

pardes.body: The psalm is a lesson with a shape. Verses 1 to 8 announce the method and the stakes: this is teaching handed down, and the failure it guards against is the fathers' own. Verses 9 to 39 tell the first cycle, exodus and sea and rock, then craving, quotation of the complaint in verses 19 and 20, anger, and mercy that stops short. Verses 40 to 64 tell it again from a different angle, this time with the plagues of Egypt, the conquest by measuring line, and an ending the first cycle did not have: Shiloh abandoned, the ark handed to an adversary, priests dead and widows not weeping. Verses 65 to 72 turn on a single waking. The two closing choices are stated flatly, Ephraim not chosen and Judah chosen, and no reason is given except love. Note what the psalm does not do. It never says the people repented and were forgiven. Mercy in {{38.1}} is grounded in God's character and in the observation of {{39.2}} that they are flesh, wind that goes and does not return. The relief at the end comes from a change of place and a change of shepherd, not from a change of heart in the people.

The opening claims a genre and then seems not to deliver it. Verse 2 promises {{2.1}}, a parable, and {{2.4}}, riddles, and what follows is straight narrative. One resolution is that the riddle is not in the events but in why they repeat, which is the question the psalm never answers directly. Several words in the psalm are genuinely hard. The last verb of verse 41, {{41.5}}, occurs so rarely that translators split between marking a limit, wounding, and grieving, and the older versions do not agree. The noun in verse 47, {{47.4}}, appears nowhere else in the Bible, so hail, frost and flooding have all been proposed on the strength of the parallel line alone. Verse 65 is the most exposed line in the book: God {{65.0}}, wakes, like a sleeper and like a fighter loud with wine. Ancient and medieval readers were uncomfortable enough with it to reach for figurative readings, and the Hebrew itself gives no signal that it is anything but a simile squarely stated. Watch also the vocabulary of turning, which stitches the whole psalm: Ephraim turns back in battle in verse 9, the people turn back in repentance in verse 34, they turn back in betrayal in verse 57, and God turns His anger back in verse 38.

The psalm hands later readers a hard question and no answer, which is exactly the condition midrash works in. Why Ephraim, when nothing in the story of the exodus singles that tribe out? Readings offered over the centuries include a premature attempt to leave Egypt before the appointed time, the location of the shrine at Shiloh in Ephraimite territory, and the northern kingdom's later history read backward into its ancestor, since Ephraim is the standard name for the north in the prophets. The psalm supports the second and third without stating either. A second question the tradition presses: what is the status of the repentance in verses 34 and 35, which the psalm demolishes two lines later as flattery? It has been read as a warning that returning under duress is not returning, and also, more generously, as evidence that even a repentance made of fear is registered, since the God of verse 38 keeps pardoning people whose hearts verse 37 says are not steady. A third reading takes the whole psalm as an argument for Jerusalem addressed to an audience that remembered Shiloh, in which case the recital of sin is not accusation but proof that the transfer of the sanctuary was earned rather than arbitrary.

Read mystically the psalm is about two names and the traffic between them. Judgement and mercy alternate through it without resolution, and the alternation is the structure rather than a defect in it. Verse 38 is the axis: pardon, restraint, anger turned back before it is fully roused, which is read as strict measure deliberately held under its own capacity so that a world can keep standing. The image of not rousing all the wrath implies a wrath that has more in it, and the mystical readings take that surplus seriously rather than as a figure of speech. Verse 65 becomes, in this register, an account of concealment and its end: the sleeper is not absent but withdrawn, and waking describes the return of an attention that never actually left. The final movement is then not a reward but a repair. The shepherd of verse 52 is God and the shepherd of verse 71 is a man, and the same verb covers both, which is read as the pattern by which what is above works through what is below. Verse 72 places the whole thing in a human heart and a pair of hands, and ends the psalm on the word for leading rather than on any word for arriving.
